title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: Vaisheshika's list of what the world is made of ends with two items that aren't stuff at all: the self, and a mind that can only hold one thing at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaisheshika, six kinds of thing in one falling mango, and the habit of seeing the seams: the person, the mood, the action. Did someone's mood pass while the person stayed? Today closes a week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

You're on the phone, nodding along, and at the same time you're reading an email. Then the voice on the phone says, "So what do you think?" And there's a little gap. You heard every word. Or did you? The sound reached your ears. The words were there. But somewhere, something wasn't connecting. Vaisheshika had no phones, but it noticed that kind of gap, and used it as evidence. That gap, the school said, is how you know there's a mind. Today the school finishes its list of what the world is made of, and the last two items are you.
screen: `ON THE PHONE, READING EMAIL.` → `"SO WHAT DO YOU THINK?"` → `THE GAP IS EVIDENCE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's first category was substance. The Vaisheshika Sutra names nine substances. Earth, water, fire, air: the four kinds of atom we met two days ago. Then akasha, the space that carries sound. Then time, and direction, which let us say before and after, here and there. And last, two that aren't stuff at all: the self, atman, and the mind, manas. Start with the self. How do you know there is one? The Sutra lists its marks, and the first is breathing out and breathing in. Then the eyelids opening and closing, life itself, the movement of the mind, and pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort. Breath is a sign of the self. Now the mind. Here's the Sutra's evidence: sometimes self, senses and object are all in contact, and still no knowing happens. The phone was talking. The ears were working. And you didn't take it in. Something has to be the gate, and that gate is the mind. In this school the mind is tiny, so it can join only one sense at a time. On this view, nobody truly reads the email and hears the call at once. The mind only switches, quickly, back and forth. And so the week closes. Nyaya gave us five steps said out loud, three kinds of talk, reasons that only look like reasons, and doubt as a doorway. Vaisheshika gave us dharma at the start, the atoms, the seams. And at the end of its list, a breathing self and a mind that can only hold one thing at a time.
screen: `NINE SUBSTANCES.` · `BREATH IS A SIGN OF THE SELF.` · `THE MIND: ONE THING AT A TIME.` · `A WEEK OF NYAYA AND VAISHESHIKA.` · then, large: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the mind hold one thing. Settle, and close your eyes or lower your gaze. Feel the breath going out and coming in, the first mark of the self in the Sutra's list. Stay with that one thing. When a sound comes, notice that the breath slipped away while you heard it. That's the gate swinging. No problem. Swing it back to the breath. Toward the end, let the eyelids open and close once, slowly, and notice that too. If you pray, you can let each breath be offered, one at a time. The bell holds the time.
Vaisheshika. Its nine substances end with the self, known by signs like breathing, and the mind, a gate that lets in one thing at a time.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Today, in one conversation, put everything else down and give the gate to one person. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the nine substances, from earth to mind, as part of the school's list of categories, and the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition uses the self's marks in its arguments that the self is real.

fork.setup: you're on the phone and reading an email. the voice says, "so what do you think?" and you've got nothing. what does Vaisheshika say just happened?
options: the mind, a gate for one sense at a time, was on the email.
nothing: you heard it all perfectly.
fork.reveal: the Sutra uses exactly this gap as evidence for the mind: self, senses and object can all be in contact and still no knowing happens.

original.note: Sanskrit: manas, the mind; in Vaisheshika, a substance that joins one sense at a time.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of what the world is made of would be all rocks and water.
what it means: Vaisheshika's nine substances end with the self and the mind, and the mind is a gate that lets in one thing at a time.
what a scholar hears: Vaisheshika Sutra 3.2.1 gives the mark of manas as the arising or non-arising of knowledge; 3.2.4 lists breathing and the rest as marks of the self.

notes: Editor pass: removed lines telling the listener what they feel ('awful little gap', 'might surprise you') and the 'long before' time claim; the one-sense-at-a-time point is now framed as the school's view, not said to the listener as fact.
Week end (days 1163–1169): the look-back names Nyaya 1162–1165 (five members, three kinds of talk, hetvabhasa, doubt) and Vaisheshika 1166–1168.
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.5 lists nine dravyas (prthivi, ap, tejas, vayu, akasha, kala, dik, atman, manas): confirm the reference.

Marks of the self, Vaisheshika Sutra 3.2.4: prana/apana, nimesha/unmesha, life, movement of mind, affections of other senses, sukha, duhkha, iccha, dvesha, prayatna. Paraphrased; confirm the list and order ('the first is breathing out and breathing in').

Mark of mind, 3.2.1: knowledge arising or not despite contact of self, sense and object. The atomic size of manas and one-sense-at-a-time are standard Nyaya-Vaisheshika teaching (compare Nyaya Sutra 1.1.16 and 3.2.56ff); confirm phrasing 'tiny'.
Akasha described as 'the space that carries sound' (sound as its quality) and dik as 'direction': confirm the glosses.
